Also 'dì' (aunt) and singular 'họ' for the owner are flagged. [Reviewer changed: Đó chỉ là một chiếc túi, nhưng → Chỉ có một chiếc túi, nhưng]
read.sections.0.text.source: Look at the woven bag in the evidence. The seller says it is made for carrying food and books. That is its practical use. The owner says an aunt gave it to them when they started at a new school, so the bag also holds a memory. The makers, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. It is one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need its context: who made it, who uses it, and why.
read.sections.0.text.back: Look at the woven bag in the evidence section. The seller says the bag was made for carrying food and books. That is its practical use. The owner says an aunt gave the bag to them when they started at a new school, so the bag also holds a memory. The people who made the bag, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. It is only a bag, but each person looks at it from a different point of view. To understand an object, you need to know its context: who made it, who used it, and why.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Objects carry meaning around the world
read.sections.1.heading.back: Objects carry meaning all over the world

read.sections.1.text.note: Ghana, Indonesia, Tonga, Fiji, Thái Bình Dương. 'tục ngữ' for proverbs, 'khăn địu em bé' for cloths that carry babies, 'vải tapa' and 'batik' kept as borrowed words. Check cultural accuracy of each description.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips that are sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used through life, from cloths that carry babies to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and it is used at weddings and other big events.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used throughout a person's life, from baby-carrying cloths to wedding clothes. In the Pacific, in places like Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and the cloth is used at weddings and other big events.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Many groups make things with cultural meaning. In Ghana, people weave kente cloth. Many kente patterns have names. Some names come from wise words or past events. In Indonesia, people make batik with wax and dye. They use it for babies and at weddings. In the Pacific, people make tapa cloth from tree bark. Groups often make it together. They use it at big events.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Many groups of people make things with cultural meaning. In Ghana, people weave kente cloth. Many kente patterns have names. Some names come from wise sayings or events in the past. In Indonesia, people make batik with wax and dye. They use it for babies and at weddings. In the Pacific, people make tapa cloth from tree bark. Groups often make it together. They use it at big events.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Ask before you explain an object

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Việc đoán xem hoa văn có nghĩa gì cũng là một sai lầm': 'sai lầm' is about the label writer, not the learner; check tone. | Review: 'nhãn yếu' (weak label) stiff; see read.checks.1.question.
read.sections.2.text.source: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag says only “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true, but it misses the memory and the skill. It is also a mistake to guess what the pattern means. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, with no source, is weak. People in one group may not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.text.back: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The bag's first label says only "Handbag for everyday use". That is true, but it leaves out the memory and the skill. Guessing what the pattern means is also a mistake. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, without a source, is a weak label. People in the same group may not see an object the same way. A better label uses evidence from the people who made and used it. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A museum label tells people about a thing. This label says “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true. But it misses the memory and the skill. Do not guess what the pattern means. Do not call it a symbol of a whole group. You need proof for that. A good label uses what the makers and users say. It also says what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: A museum label tells people about an object. This label says "Handbag for everyday use". That is true. But it leaves out the memory and the skill. Do not guess what the pattern means. Do not call it a symbol of a whole group of people. You need evidence for that. A good label uses what the makers and users say. It also says what we still need to ask.

'trao đổi hàng' for traded. Check each, including the historical statement about trade with China. | Review: 'pot' rendered 'bình' (jar/vase) and 'handkerchief' 'khăn tay'; 'Philippines' is written in English form (Phi-líp-pin is also common). Check names of objects.
watch.summary.source: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded for Chinese pots and bowls. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shell and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem sewn into it. The video says the materials and the skill make an object valuable. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.
watch.summary.back: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. The video is about three everyday objects of the museum. The first object is a small green jar from China. In the past, people in the Philippines traded goods to get Chinese jars and bowls. Most were simple, but this one has two dragons. The second object is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shells and silver for important people. The third object is a small piece of cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem embroidered on it. The video says material and skill give an object value. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.
